hook: two in the morning in a temple courtyard: the hardest hour, and a song that wakes everyone up

segments.voice: Yesterday in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: the fast, which clears space and turns each pang into a bell. When a craving rang, what did you answer? A new week begins, and the night goes on. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.
screen: `THE FAST: HUNGER AS A BELL.` · `A NEW WEEK, THE SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: It's a little before two in the morning, in a temple courtyard. The crowd that pushed through the gates at sunset has thinned. People sit on mats against the walls. A child sleeps across her grandmother's lap. A man in a shawl has been nodding for ten minutes, catching himself, nodding again. The lamps are lower. Even the drummer looks tired. Hours like this one decide whether a vigil is kept or quietly given up. Then somebody near the shrine starts a new song, loud, with a call everyone knows how to answer. Heads lift. The man in the shawl sits up and sings. Today's lesson in the night curriculum is that hour.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `THE HARDEST HOUR.` → `SOMEBODY STARTS A SONG.`

segments.voice: Keeping awake on this night has a name: jagarana, wakefulness, the vigil. It's the part of the Shivaratri vow that gives the night its character, and it's easy to misread as a test of endurance. Look at how it's actually done, and it's something else. First, it's done together. In temples, the night is held up by singing, chanting, and rounds of worship that come one after another, so there's always something to wake into. You keep yourself awake, but you also keep the person next to you awake, and they keep you. Second, it's done on purpose. The point isn't simply not sleeping. People stay up all night for many reasons. The vigil asks you to stay up toward something, with your attention pointed at Shiva, hour after hour. And third, it points past the night. The Katha Upanishad has a call that fits this hour: arise, awake, go to the great teachers and learn. It warns that the path is as sharp as a razor's edge, hard to walk. That wakefulness isn't about eyelids. But the body staying awake on this one night is a way of rehearsing the other kind, the kind of waking up the Upanishad means. So the courtyard at two in the morning is a small picture of the whole teaching. Everyone is tired. Nobody is awake by their own strength alone. And the thing that lifts the heads isn't a scolding. It's a song someone was willing to start. Which means sometimes, in the hard hour, the lesson isn't to stay awake. It's to be the one who starts the song.
screen: `JAGARANA: THE VIGIL.` · `KEPT AWAKE TOGETHER.` · `AWAKE TOWARD SOMETHING.` · `ARISE, AWAKE, AND LEARN.` · then, large: `BE THE ONE WHO STARTS THE SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: an awake sit. Sit up a little straighter than usual, spine tall, and if you like, keep the eyes just slightly open, resting on a spot in front of you. Breathe. At some point the mind will start to drift or dull, the way heads nod at two in the morning. When you notice it, don't scold yourself. Lift. Straighten the back, take one fuller breath, and come back. Every lift is a small vigil. If you pray, you can let Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, be the song that lifts you. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson three: jagarana, the vigil, wakefulness kept together and pointed toward Shiva, a rehearsal for waking up.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Today, when someone near you is flagging, at work or at home, be the one who starts the song. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep the jagarana stay awake through the night, in temples or at home, with bhajans, chanting of Om Namah Shivaya, and rounds of worship of the linga until dawn.

fork.setup: it's two in the morning in the temple courtyard. the person beside you keeps nodding off. what do you do?
options: let them sleep; it's their vow, not yours.
start the next song, or sing it with them.
slip out quietly so you don't disturb anyone.
fork.reveal: on this night wakefulness is shared. nobody stays up by their own strength alone, and a song is how a tired crowd lifts its head.

what it means: staying awake together, on purpose, with attention pointed at Shiva until dawn.
what a scholar hears: the Katha Upanishad's call to arise and awake, and its warning that the path is sharp as a razor's edge; the body's vigil rehearses that waking.
